analysis.one_liner: Lets states cut Medicaid and children's health coverage eligibility below federally protected levels.
analysis.headline: Introduced by 26 Senate Republicans, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the 'maintenance of effort' rules that came with the 2009 stimulus law and the 2010 health law. Those rules barred states from making Medicaid and CHIP eligibility stricter than the standards in place in 2008 and 2010 — a condition of the extra federal money and an anti-rollback protection under the health law. The bill would let states cut eligibility, reduce enrollment, and save state money, while low-income families and children could lose or never gain coverage. The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee, which took no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: State governments that want to shrink Medicaid and CHIP rolls and budgets. Freed from the maintenance-of-effort rules, states could tighten eligibility below the 2008 and 2010 standards and reduce their share of program costs. Fiscal conservatives in Congress would also see federal and state health spending pressure ease, since coverage protections would no longer be guaranteed.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ARRA maintenance-of-effort requirement that barred states from making Medicaid eligibility more restrictive than the standards in effect on July 1, 2008, and the PPACA requirements protecting 2010 standards for Medicaid and CHIP.
Gives states freedom to tighten eligibility standards, methodologies, and procedures — which would let them cut program enrollment and state spending.

analysis.who_pays: Low-income families and children who rely on Medicaid and CHIP. If states tightened eligibility after the rules were repealed, people who would have qualified under the protected standards could be denied coverage, and the federal guarantee that stimulus and health-law funds would not pay for coverage cuts would be gone.

drawbacks.text: The maintenance-of-effort rules were the federal backstop preventing states from cutting Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for low-income people; repealing them removes that protection and could leave families and children uninsured.

The protections were attached to enhanced federal Medicaid funding under the stimulus law; letting states keep the funding while cutting eligibility shifts costs onto the federal government and other taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: States would gain real budget flexibility, and some argue they were best positioned to decide who their programs cover. The cost falls on the people with the least ability to absorb it: the rules being repealed exist precisely to stop states from cutting coverage for poor families and children while drawing enhanced federal funds. This is a savings bill whose savings come out of low-income people's health coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it twice and sent it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Hatch introduced the bill on May 3, 2011, joined by seven original cosponsors.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 112th Congress.
By the time the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, the bill had died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income families on Medicaid and CHIP, who kept the federal protection against state eligibility cuts. State budgets remained unchanged because the flexibility the bill offered was never enacted.

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 3, 2011, to repeal the ARRA and PPACA Medicaid and CHIP maintenance-of-effort requirements.

for.name: 25 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 26 Republican senators.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the Finance Committee took no action after it was referred on May 3, 2011.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and a Democratic-controlled Senate committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: Repealing the maintenance-of-effort rules would free states to tighten Medicaid and CHIP eligibility and cut program spending, with the cost falling on low-income residents who lose coverage. The savings would come directly at ordinary beneficiaries' expense.

After 2014, people cut from Medicaid could shift onto subsidized private exchange plans, which would route customers to insurers; but wholesale eligibility tightening would also shrink covered populations overall. The mechanism cuts both ways.
